Would you tell a student how many people hold access, and whether you would support removal?

subject: Putting the storage limit into the contract itself
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

A policy on a web page can be edited on a quiet afternoon. Terms in a signed agreement cannot. If {{city}} means to hold the vendor to any storage limit for scans taken near {{shortName}}, I think that limit belongs in the contract with a remedy attached, rather than in a document the company controls.

Anything weaker reads to me as a preference dressed up as a rule.

My own preference is stronger still. I would like the automated plate readers around campus taken out of service, with nothing approved to replace them.

Would you check whether the retention limit appears in the agreement, and reply to a student with your position on removal?

subject: Getting the data back if the city walks away
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

Exit terms decide who holds the leverage. Should {{city}} choose not to renew, is there a defined process for retrieving or destroying the scans gathered around {{shortName}}, and does the city have any way to enforce it against a company that would rather keep the archive?

Without that, non renewal would end the service while leaving the record in private hands indefinitely, which is the outcome I would least like to see.

The cleanest version ends both at once. I am asking you to support removing the automated plate readers around campus with no new ones approved, and to require written confirmation that the existing data has been destroyed.

Could you tell a student what the exit provisions say, and where you stand?

subject: The stored scans look like a standing liability
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

Treat this as a risk question and it gets simpler. The archive of plate reads near {{shortName}} is an asset to nobody and an exposure to the city every day it exists. It generates obligations without generating revenue, and its worst case is far larger than its best case.

Any other municipal holding with that profile would be wound down on advice from counsel, which is why I find its continuation puzzling rather than sinister.

I am asking for the same treatment here. I would like the automated plate readers around campus removed and no new ones installed, and then the exposure goes to nothing.

Would you raise this as a liability question and let a student know your view?

subject: Would you support a public session on storage
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

This seems to deserve a session of its own rather than a line item buried in a longer agenda. Storage periods, access lists, audit practice, and destruction procedures for the records gathered around {{shortName}} are all matters residents of {{city}} could reasonably weigh in on, and none of them has been aired.

A hearing would surface things a letter from a student cannot.

I will state my position now so it is not a surprise later. I would like the automated plate readers around campus removed, and no new ones approved anywhere near it.

Would you support scheduling such a session, and would you tell me how you would vote on removal?

subject: Two questions about the plate reader archive
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

Two questions, and I will keep them short.

First, how long are the scans collected around {{shortName}} retained, and is that period set by {{city}} or by the company operating the system? Second, is every search of that archive logged in a way that someone outside the department can review?

I have not been able to answer either from public sources, which seems like a problem for a program funded with public money, and it is why a student is writing to you about it.

My position does not depend on the answers. I would like the automated plate readers around campus taken out, with none installed in their place.

A reply on the two questions and on your own position would be genuinely useful to me.

subject: Removal would settle every question about storage
body:
Dear {{officialName}},

Every difficult question about this program dissolves at the same point. How long records are kept, who may search them, what happens when the company is acquired, who answers if the store is breached. All of it becomes moot the moment the collection stops.

That is the unusual feature of surveillance data, at least as I understand it. The problems are not weighed against the benefits so much as created by the decision to retain.

With {{readersInState}} readers now operating across {{state}}, the accumulation is not slowing on its own. I hope you will support removing the automated plate readers around campus and approving no new ones in {{city}}.

I would like to know your position, and as one student I will take a clear no as a real answer.
